Builds on [page 1, the spring](oscillator.qmd). About 2 minutes for the puzzle and the gist; about 20 with the mathematics, plus the folds.
:::

::: {.puzzle}
Thread beads on a tight string and join the ends into a ring. Pluck one bead and the ring wobbles in a tangle, and sounds like a jangle. Start it in just the right shape, though, and it swings cleanly and sounds one pure tone. Where were the clean tones hiding in the jangle?
:::

Press "Hear this motion" on the tangle. Then press a mode button and hear it again.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <canvas id="rCanvas" style="height:300px" aria-label="Beads on a ring, displacements drawn in and out of the circle"></canvas>
  <div class="slider"><label for="rN">Beads</label><input type="range" id="rN" min="3" max="24" step="1" value="8"><output id="rNo"></output></div>
  <div class="controls" id="rModes" role="group" aria-label="Play one mode"></div>
  <div class="controls"><button id="rPluck">Pluck one bead</button><button id="rPlay" class="primary">Hear this motion</button></div>
  <svg class="spec" id="rSpec" viewBox="0 0 320 100" style="max-width:520px" aria-label="Frequencies of the modes relative to the lowest"></svg>
  <div class="readout" id="rRead"></div>
  <p class="cap">Mode k is a wave that fits k times around the ring; in mode 0 all the beads just move together. The beads are drawn moving in and out of the circle; real ones move out of the page.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

::: {.gist}
**The gist.** Each clean tone is a wave that fits a whole number of times around the ring. In it, every bead swings at the same frequency and the shape never changes, as if the whole ring were one mass on a spring. Such a motion is called a [mode](glossary.qmd#mode). The tangle is all the modes at once, each at its own frequency: a chord. Below, Newton's law turns the ring into an operator, a matrix, and that matrix's eigenvectors are the clean tones.
:::

## The operator

As on page 1, apply Newton's law to one piece of the instrument, here one bead, and find the force. It will turn out to depend on the bead's neighbors as well as on the bead itself, so the rule that turns the shape into the force acts on all the beads at once.

Let $u_j$ be the height of bead $j$, with $N$ beads, each of mass $m$, spaced $h$ apart along a string of tension $T$. Because the loop closes, bead $N$ is next to bead 1, so bead numbers are counted around the ring. (This is an idealization: a real loop of string would need something to hold it out against its own tension. The model keeps only the sideways pulls between neighbors, exactly as for a straight string whose two ends are joined.)

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 420 160" role="img" aria-label="A bead pulled by the string toward its two neighbors">
  <path class="dash" d="M 20 120 L 400 120"/>
  <path class="ink" d="M 60 110 L 210 60 L 360 100"/>
  <circle cx="60" cy="110" r="6" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="210" cy="60" r="7" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="360" cy="100" r="6" class="fillacc"/>
  <path class="pos" d="M 210 60 L 150 80"/><path class="pos" d="M 210 60 L 270 76"/>
  <path class="neg" d="M 210 60 L 210 110"/>
  <text x="40" y="140">bead j−1</text><text x="190" y="40">bead j</text><text x="340" y="140">bead j+1</text>
  <text x="120" y="76">T</text><text x="280" y="70">T</text><text x="218" y="100">net pull</text>
</svg>
```

**1. One side's pull.** The string between beads $j$ and $j+1$ pulls bead $j$ along itself with force $T$. That piece of string rises by $u_{j+1} - u_j$ over a distance $h$, so its slope is $(u_{j+1} - u_j)/h$. If $\theta$ is the angle it makes with the horizontal, then for small slopes the vertical part of the pull is
$$
T\sin\theta \approx T\tan\theta = \frac{T}{h}\,(u_{j+1} - u_j) .
$$

**2. The other side.** The string on the other side pulls in the same way, with vertical part
$$
\frac{T}{h}\,(u_{j-1} - u_j) .
$$

**3. Newton's law for one bead.** Adding the two pulls and setting the total equal to mass times acceleration,
$$
m\,\ddot u_j = \frac{T}{h}\left(u_{j+1} - 2u_j + u_{j-1}\right).
$$
The bracket is twice the gap between the average of the two neighbors and bead $j$ itself: a bead sitting above its neighbors is pulled down, one sitting below is pulled up. So each bead is a mass on a spring, except that where its spring pulls it depends on where its neighbors are.

**4. All the beads at once.** Collect the heights into one column $u = (u_1, \dots, u_N)$. The $N$ equations become one,
$$
\ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}\,K\,u ,
$$
where $K$ is the $N\times N$ matrix with 2 on the diagonal, $-1$ just above and below it, and $-1$ in the two corners, because bead 1 and bead $N$ are neighbors. For $N = 5$,
$$
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 & 0 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & -1 & 2 & -1 & 0\\ 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & 0 & 0 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Here $Ku$ is the column whose $j$-th entry is row $j$ of $K$ times $u$: multiply each entry of row $j$ by the matching entry of $u$, and add. Row $j$ has 2 in place $j$ and $-1$ in places $j - 1$ and $j + 1$, so $(Ku)_j = 2u_j - u_{j-1} - u_{j+1}$, which is the bead equation for every bead at once. Each row of $K$ is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around; a matrix with this property is called [circulant](glossary.qmd#circulant).

::: {.result}
**The operator.**
$$
\ddot u = -A\,u, \qquad A = \frac{T}{mh}\,K ,
$$
a matrix acting on the list of all the beads' heights. On page 1 the operator was one number; here it is a table of numbers.
:::

**What we assumed.** Small slopes, a tension that does not change as the string flexes, point-like beads on a massless string, and the idealized closed ring described above.

## Its spectrum

A mode is a shape that keeps its form while it swings. Most starting shapes change as they move: that is the tangle. But in a few special shapes, every bead is pulled back in proportion to its own height, by the same factor for every bead. Then every bead is a mass on the same spring, they all swing in step, and the shape only grows and shrinks. In matrix language, a nonzero column $v$ is an [eigenvector](glossary.qmd#eigenvector) of $K$, with [eigenvalue](glossary.qmd#eigenvalue) $\lambda$, if
$$
K v = \lambda\, v ,
$$
so the matrix only rescales it, possibly by zero. The list of all the eigenvalues is the matrix's [spectrum](glossary.qmd#spectrum).

**1. Each eigenvector is a mode.** If $Kv = \lambda v$, try $u(t) = v\cos(\omega t)$. Differentiating twice gives $\ddot u = -\omega^2 v\cos\omega t$, while $-\frac{T}{mh}Ku = -\frac{T}{mh}\lambda\, v\cos\omega t$. These agree when
$$
\omega^2 = \frac{T}{mh}\,\lambda .
$$
Every bead swings at the same [angular frequency](glossary.qmd#angular-frequency) $\omega$ (radians per second; page 1), in the fixed shape $v$: the mass on a spring again, once for each eigenvector.

**2. A small example, three beads.** For $N = 3$,
$$
K = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 & -1\\ -1 & 2 & -1\\ -1 & -1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Row $j$ gives $(Kv)_j = 3v_j - (v_1 + v_2 + v_3)$. The column $(1, 1, 1)$ gives $K(1,1,1) = (0,0,0)$: an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0. Every bead moves up together, nothing stretches, nothing pulls back, and the frequency is 0, so the ring just drifts; this is the mode 0 of the demo. Any column whose entries add up to zero gives $(Kv)_j = 3v_j$, so $Kv = 3v$. Every such column is a combination $a(1, -1, 0) + b(0, 1, -1)$, so these eigenvectors fill a whole plane: every one is built from those two shapes, and neither of the two is a multiple of the other. The eigenvalues are $0, 3, 3$, with 3 counted twice: it has [multiplicity](glossary.qmd#multiplicity) 2.

**3. Any number of beads: the modes are waves.** On a ring no bead is special, so try waves that fit a whole number of times around: $v_j = \cos(2\pi jk/N)$, a wave with $k$ crests. The identity $\cos(a + b) + \cos(a - b) = 2\cos a\cos b$, with $a = 2\pi jk/N$ and $b = 2\pi k/N$, gives $v_{j+1} + v_{j-1} = 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\,v_j$, so
$$
\begin{aligned}
(Kv)_j &= 2v_j - v_{j+1} - v_{j-1} \\
&= \big(2 - 2\cos(2\pi k/N)\big)\,v_j \\
&= 4\sin^2\!\Big(\frac{\pi k}{N}\Big)\,v_j ,
\end{aligned}
$$
using $1 - \cos 2x = 2\sin^2 x$. The same holds for $v_j = \sin(2\pi jk/N)$. These are the shapes the mode buttons play. At the beads, a wave with $N - k$ crests looks exactly like one with $k$ crests (the cosine is the same and the sine changes sign), so the different eigenvalues come from $k = 0, 1, \dots$ up to $N/2$, rounded down, and each one from $k = 1$ up to just below $N/2$ has two eigenvectors, a cosine and a sine. (At $k = 0$, and at $k = N/2$ when $N$ is even, the sine is zero at every bead, so only the cosine is left.) A wave with more crests bends more sharply from bead to bead, so each bead is pulled back harder and the wave swings faster.

::: {.result}
**The spectrum.** Eigenvectors: the waves $\cos(2\pi jk/N)$ and $\sin(2\pi jk/N)$ with $k$ crests. Eigenvalues of $K$: $4\sin^2(\pi k/N)$. Angular frequencies: $\omega_k = 2\sqrt{T/(mh)}\,\sin(\pi k/N)$, so mode $k$ sounds at $\sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N)$ times mode 1.
:::

In the 1730s Daniel Bernoulli studied systems like this, weights strung along a flexible thread and a hanging chain, and came to believe that every vibration is built from such simple motions; in 1753 he put this forward as a general principle. For the beads it is a theorem, and writing a motion as a sum of these waves is the [discrete Fourier transform](glossary.qmd#dft).

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Proof</span>Every motion is a sum of modes <span class="needs">uses linear algebra</span></summary>

The matrix $K$ is symmetric: the entry in row $i$, column $j$ equals the entry in row $j$, column $i$. By the [spectral theorem for symmetric matrices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem), $K$ has a basis of $N$ mutually [orthogonal](glossary.qmd#orthogonal) (perpendicular) eigenvectors $v^{(1)}, \dots, v^{(N)}$ with real eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_N$. Write the motion as $u(t) = \sum_k a_k(t)\,v^{(k)}$. Substituting into $\ddot u = -\frac{T}{mh}Ku$ and taking the dot product with $v^{(k)}$, which removes every other term because they are perpendicular, gives $\ddot a_k = -\omega_k^2 a_k$ with $\omega_k^2 = \frac{T}{mh}\lambda_k$: each coefficient obeys its own mass-on-a-spring equation. With starting shape $u(0) = \sum_k c_k v^{(k)}$ and starting velocity $\dot u(0) = \sum_k d_k v^{(k)}$, and by the uniqueness of solutions from page 1, every motion is $u(t) = \sum_k \big(c_k\cos\omega_k t + \frac{d_k}{\omega_k}\sin\omega_k t\big)v^{(k)}$, read as $c_k + d_k t$ when $\omega_k = 0$. The eigenvalues are nonnegative because $u \cdot Ku = \sum_j u_j(2u_j - u_{j+1} - u_{j-1}) = \sum_j (u_{j+1} - u_j)^2 \ge 0$, by regrouping the terms around the ring; for an eigenvector this equals $\lambda\,(u\cdot u)$.

</details>
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>The same waves, written with complex numbers <span class="needs">uses complex numbers</span></summary>

With [Euler's formula](glossary.qmd#euler-formula) $e^{ix} = \cos x + i\sin x$, the cosine and sine waves combine into $v_j = e^{2\pi i jk/N}$ for $k = 0, 1, \dots, N - 1$ (here $i$ is the imaginary unit and $j$ the bead number). Then $(Kv)_j = \big(2 - e^{2\pi ik/N} - e^{-2\pi ik/N}\big)v_j = 4\sin^2(\pi k/N)\,v_j$ in one line. These $N$ waves are the basis vectors of the discrete Fourier transform, and they are eigenvectors of every circulant matrix, not only this one. Combined with the time factor $e^{\mp i\omega t}$, the waves with $k$ and $N - k$ crests travel around the ring in opposite directions.

</details>
:::

## On the pitch ruler

The stems are the modes' frequencies from the result box, as multiples of mode 1's, the slowest wave that swings back and forth. Each stem's height is how much of that mode the current motion contains. Apart from mode 1 itself, they generally miss the lines. With 8 beads, as the demo starts, the modes sit at 1×, 1.85×, 2.41× and 2.61×. Raise the number of beads and the low stems close in on the lines: with 24 beads, modes 2 and 3 are within 2.5% of 2× and 3×. The high modes stay far off.

## What the spectrum explains

**The jangle is a chord.** Pluck one bead and the starting shape is not a wave; but it is a sum of waves, and each wave swings at its own frequency, $\omega_k$, as if it were alone. So the plucked ring sounds all those frequencies at once. They sit off the lines, so the chord is a jangle. Start the ring in one wave's shape and only that one frequency sounds: a pure tone. The clean tones were in the jangle all along, as its eigenvectors.

**Almost whole numbers.** A long wave, with few crests, spreads over many beads, and to it the beads look like a smooth string; its frequency grows in step with its number of crests, almost exactly as whole numbers do. A short wave, with crests only a bead or two apart, feels the gaps between the beads, and its frequency falls behind. That is why the low stems sit near the lines and close in as you add beads, while the high ones stay off.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>How near to whole numbers <span class="needs">uses the sine function</span></summary>

Mode $k$ has angular frequency $\omega_k = 2\sqrt{T/(mh)}\,\sin(\pi k/N)$, so its frequency is proportional to $\sin(\pi k/N)$, which is not proportional to $k$: the beads are not exactly harmonic. For small $k$, $\sin(\pi k/N) \approx \pi k/N$, so the low modes are nearly harmonic, and the ratio $\sin(\pi k/N)/\sin(\pi/N)$ tends to $k$ as $N$ grows. The modes near $k = N/2$ stay far from the whole-number grid: for an even number of beads the largest ratio is $1/\sin(\pi/N)$ (slightly less for an odd number), and for any number of beads it is about $N/\pi$ once there are many, not $N/2$. A mode can land on a line by coincidence: with 6 beads, the top mode sits at exactly 2×.

</details>
:::

## What we found

Newton's law for each bead gave the ring's operator: the matrix $\frac{T}{mh}K$, acting on the list of heights. Its eigenvectors are waves around the ring, its eigenvalues are $4\sin^2(\pi k/N)$ times $T/(mh)$, and their square roots give the modes' frequencies. Any motion, even a tangle, is a sum of modes: a chord. On a ring the low modes sit near the lines of the pitch ruler, but not on them.

## The next puzzle

The beads' low frequencies creep toward the lines as you add beads. With infinitely many, a continuous loop of string, do they land on them exactly?

```{=html}
<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, N = 8, a = [], b = [], u0 = null, t0 = performance.now(), mode = 1;
  var cv = document.getElementById("rCanvas"), ctx = cv.getContext("2d");
  function lam(k) { return 4 * Math.pow(Math.sin(Math.PI * k / N), 2); }
  function ratio(k) { return Math.sin(Math.PI * k / N) / Math.sin(Math.PI / N); }
  function setMode(k) {
    mode = k; a = []; b = []; for (var q = 0; q < N; q++) { a.push(0); b.push(0); }
    a[k] = 1; t0 = performance.now(); buttons(); spec();
  }
  function pluck() {
    // bead 0 pushed out by 1, the others at rest: u_j = (1/N) sum_k e^{2 pi i jk/N}, folded into cosines
    mode = -1; a = []; b = [];
    for (var k = 0; k < N; k++) { a.push(k === 0 ? 1 / N : (2 * k < N ? 2 / N : 0)); b.push(0); }
    if (N % 2 === 0) a[N / 2] = 1 / N;
    t0 = performance.now(); buttons(); spec();
  }
  function shape(t) {
    var u = [];
    for (var j = 0; j < N; j++) {
      var s = 0;
      for (var k = 0; k <= Math.floor(N / 2); k++) {
        var w = 2 * Math.PI * 0.35 * ratio(k), c = Math.cos(w * t);
        s += (a[k] * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * j * k / N) + b[k] * Math.sin(2 * Math.PI * j * k / N)) * (k === 0 ? 1 : c);
      }
      u.push(s);
    }
    return u;
  }
  function buttons() {
    var box = document.getElementById("rModes"); box.innerHTML = "";
    for (var k = 0; k <= Math.floor(N / 2); k++) (function (k) {
      var bt = document.createElement("button"); bt.type = "button"; bt.textContent = "mode " + k; bt.setAttribute("aria-pressed", k === mode);
      bt.addEventListener("click", function () { setMode(k); }); box.appendChild(bt);
    })(k);
  }
  function spec() {
    var parts = [];
    for (var k = 1; k <= Math.floor(N / 2); k++) parts.push({ ratio: ratio(k), amp: Math.max(Math.abs(a[k]), Math.abs(b[k]), 0.0001) });
    C.stems(document.getElementById("rSpec"), parts, { W: 320, H: 100, rmax: Math.max(4, Math.ceil(ratio(Math.floor(N / 2)))), fs: 8, sw: 3 });
    var r = []; for (var k = 1; k <= Math.min(5, Math.floor(N / 2)); k++) r.push(ratio(k).toFixed(2) + "×");
    document.getElementById("rRead").innerHTML = N + " beads · modes 1 to " + r.length + " at <b>" + r.join(", ") + "</b> the lowest" + (mode === 0 ? " · mode 0: the whole ring shifts together; nothing pulls it back, so it does not swing at all" : "");
  }
  function draw(now) {
    var d = C.fit(cv), W = cv.width, H = cv.height, cx = W / 2, cy = H / 2, R = Math.min(W, H) * 0.32, t = (now - t0) / 1000, u = shape(t), mx = 1;
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); ctx.lineWidth = d; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(cx, cy, R, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--muted"); ctx.lineWidth = 1.5 * d; ctx.beginPath();
    for (var j = 0; j <= N; j++) { var jj = j % N, th = 2 * Math.PI * jj / N - Math.PI / 2, r = R + u[jj] / mx * R * 0.28, x = cx + r * Math.cos(th), y = cy + r * Math.sin(th); if (j) ctx.lineTo(x, y); else ctx.moveTo(x, y); }
    ctx.stroke();
    for (var j = 0; j < N; j++) { var th = 2 * Math.PI * j / N - Math.PI / 2, r = R + u[j] / mx * R * 0.28; ctx.fillStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(cx + r * Math.cos(th), cy + r * Math.sin(th), 6 * d, 0, 2 * Math.PI); ctx.fill(); }
    requestAnimationFrame(draw);
  }
  document.getElementById("rPlay").addEventListener("click", function () {
    // the model has no friction; the sound is faded out only so that it stops
    var parts = []; for (var k = 1; k <= Math.floor(N / 2); k++) parts.push({ f: 196 * ratio(k), amp: Math.max(Math.abs(a[k]), Math.abs(b[k])), tau: 0.8 });
    if (!parts.some(function (p) { return p.amp > 1e-6; })) parts = [{ f: 1, amp: 0, tau: 1 }];
    C.play(C.render(parts, 2.2), 0.7);
  });
  document.getElementById("rPluck").addEventListener("click", pluck);
  var ns = document.getElementById("rN");
  ns.addEventListener("input", function () { N = parseInt(ns.value, 10); document.getElementById("rNo").textContent = N; if (mode < 0) pluck(); else setMode(Math.min(mode, Math.floor(N / 2))); });
  document.getElementById("rNo").textContent = N;
  C.onTheme(spec);
  pluck(); requestAnimationFrame(draw);
})();
</script>
```
